newsitem.title: UK: Britain denies it knew of Rwanda arms probe by UN.
newsitem.headline: Britain denies it knew of Rwanda arms probe by UN.

text.p: The British customs agency said on Monday it did not receive UN requests last year for intelligence on British companies that may have been involved in shipping arms to Rwandan Hutu rebels in Eastern Zaire.
"We were alerted only last week to the fact that the U.N. had sent requests," a spokeswoman for Britain's Customs and Excise told Reuters.
"We never received any earlier letters. The first communication we had from the U.N. was last week."
She was speaking as media reports on Monday linked a company registered in the Isle of Man with the supply of arms.

The U.N. said in a report that Britain failed to respond to letters it sent on 30 November and 18 December 1995, requesting information concerning a British-based company thought to have been involved in transporting arms to Goma.

According to the still unpublished U.N. report on arms shipments to Zaire, a copy of which was obtained earlier this month by Reuters, Rwandan Hutu rebels have been amply supplied with arms from Europe and South Africa.

The report, prepared for the U.N. Security Council by a four-man U.N.-appointed Commission of Inquiry, is part of a series documenting violations of an arms embargo imposed after the 1994 ethnic massacres against Tutsis in Rwanda.
British media reports on Monday said the Isle of Man company had been involved in the supply of arms to the former Rwandan government before and after its genocide of some one million people in 1994.

Documents found by British reporters near the abandoned Hutu refugee camp in Goma, eastern Zaire, appeared to show that the company helped to arrange shipments of mortars, rifles and heavy machinegun ammunition from third countries including Israel and Albania.
Much of the weaponry appeared to have come from former East European communist states, BBC and Times reporters said.
